words.shortDefinition: An open-source data versioning system that provides git-like branch, commit, merge, and diff operations directly on object storage (S3, GCS, Azure Blob).
words.simpleDefinition: LakeFS puts a git-like interface on top of your data lake. You can branch a dataset for an experiment, commit a snapshot when training completes, diff two training runs' input datasets, and merge a feature branch's data changes back to main — all without copying data between buckets. LakeFS stores only the metadata of which files belong to which version, so branching and committing are nearly instantaneous even for petabyte-scale datasets.
words.longDefinition: LakeFS (open-sourced by Treeverse in 2020) addresses the fundamental mismatch between data science workflows (iterative, experimental, needing reproducibility) and object storage (mutable, unversioned, no branching). It implements a data version control system with the same conceptual model as Git but designed for the operational characteristics of object storage at scale. LakeFS works by sitting as a proxy in front of existing object storage: all reads and writes go through LakeFS endpoints, which apply versioning semantics. A 'branch' in LakeFS is a pointer to a specific state of the data lake, not a copy. Creating a branch is a metadata operation (sub-second), not a data operation. A 'commit' records a snapshot of the branch state, assigning it an immutable SHA-like identifier. 'Diff' compares two commits or branches and shows which files were added, modified, or deleted. 'Merge' combines changes from one branch into another, applying conflict resolution rules. For ML, LakeFS enables: atomic training dataset snapshots (commit the exact data state before training), experiment isolation (experiment on a branch without affecting the main training data), rollback to a known-good data state when a pipeline produces bad data, and audit trails showing exactly which data version produced each model artifact. LakeFS integrates natively with Spark, Trino, dbt, and Airflow via its S3-compatible endpoint, requiring no changes to existing tooling beyond an endpoint URL change.
words.connector: Think of LakeFS like GitHub for your data lake — you can create branches for experiments, commit snapshots before training, and merge feature data back to main with a pull request, all without duplicating petabytes of data between storage buckets.
words.techContext: Our training pipeline commits the input dataset to LakeFS before each training run, linking the commit SHA to the MLflow run so every model artifact has a verifiable data provenance chain.
words.exampleSentence: LakeFS let us create a branch for the A/B dataset experiment, run training, and compare the two resulting models without any risk of corrupting the main training data — then merge or discard the branch when done.
words.etymology: Compound of 'Lake' (data lake) + 'FS' (file system); LakeFS is a file system interface over object storage with git-like version control semantics; developed and open-sourced by Treeverse, an Israeli startup, in 2020.

words.shortDefinition: Automated checks at each traffic-increase step of a gradual rollout that pause or abort the rollout if latency, error rate, or model quality metrics regress.
words.simpleDefinition: As a new model is gradually rolled out from 5% to 100% of traffic, rollout gates automatically evaluate its health at each step. If the new model's serving latency spikes, its error rate rises, or a proxy quality metric degrades beyond a threshold, the gate holds the rollout at the current percentage — or rolls back to 0% — until the team investigates. Gates turn the gradual rollout from a manual, attended process into an automated, safe deployment.
words.longDefinition: Model rollout gates are the automated quality checkpoints that make gradual rollout safe at scale. Without them, a gradual rollout requires a human to actively monitor dashboards at each traffic increment step and manually decide whether to proceed, pause, or roll back — an error-prone process that delays deployment and does not scale. Rollout gates codify the pass/fail criteria for each traffic increase as executable checks that run automatically after a bake window at each increment. A complete gate set for an ML model rollout typically includes three layers of checks. Infrastructure gates validate that the new model's serving infrastructure is healthy: request error rate, P99 serving latency, database connection pool usage, memory consumption. These are the same metrics you would gate any service deployment on. Model quality proxy gates check signals that don't require ground-truth labels: prediction score distribution stability (is the output distribution consistent with the champion?), average prediction confidence (is the model unusually uncertain?), and feature retrieval latency from the feature store. Business metric gates, where feedback arrives quickly enough, check downstream business outcomes: click-through rate, conversion rate, or transaction approval rate. Each gate has a threshold and an action: if the threshold is breached, the rollout pauses automatically and triggers an alert. After investigation and remediation, the rollout can be resumed or aborted. Rollout gates are implemented in model serving platforms like Argo Rollouts (via analysis templates), KServe (via canary traffic controls), and Flagger.
words.connector: Think of model rollout gates like automated safety interlocks on a chemical plant — each stage of the process requires a specific set of sensors to show safe readings before the next valve is opened, and any dangerous reading triggers an automatic shutdown.
words.techContext: Our rollout gate config checks p99 latency, error rate, and prediction distribution PSI at 5%, 25%, and 75% traffic; a gate failure at any step pauses the rollout and pages the on-call ML engineer.
words.exampleSentence: The 25% rollout gate detected a 2x increase in average prediction latency from the new model's larger feature vector and automatically paused the rollout, preventing the latency regression from reaching full production.

spec:

words.shortDefinition: Uber's pioneering internal ML platform (described 2017) that unified the full ML lifecycle — data, training, evaluation, serving — into a shared company-wide system.
words.simpleDefinition: Michelangelo was Uber's internal ML platform, described in a landmark 2017 blog post that effectively defined what a production ML platform should be. It unified feature engineering, training, evaluation, and model serving into a single system used by all of Uber's ML teams, eliminating the duplicated ad-hoc tooling that each team had built independently. Michelangelo's architecture — particularly its feature store and model registry — became the template for the entire MLOps tooling ecosystem.
words.longDefinition: Uber's Michelangelo platform, described by Jeremy Hermann and Mike Del Balso in 2017, is the most influential ML platform design in the industry. At the time of publication, Uber had hundreds of models in production (ETA prediction, demand forecasting, fraud detection, surge pricing) built and deployed by different teams using incompatible tooling. Michelangelo's core insight was that the most valuable investment in an ML platform is eliminating the duplication of feature computation between training and serving — which became the canonical definition of a feature store. The platform unified six capabilities into a single system: a shared feature store (with online and offline components), a model training framework (supporting XGBoost, TensorFlow, and custom Python models), an experiment tracking and model registry system, an evaluation and validation framework, a model serving infrastructure (supporting both batch and online inference), and a model monitoring layer. All ML teams at Uber used Michelangelo regardless of their use case, which drove standardization of tooling, data formats, and evaluation practices across hundreds of engineers. The paper's influence is visible across the MLOps landscape: Tecton was founded by the Michelangelo team, MLflow's model registry mirrors Michelangelo's lifecycle stages, and every major cloud ML platform (SageMaker, Vertex AI, Azure ML) implements the same architectural pattern Michelangelo demonstrated at scale.
words.connector: Think of Michelangelo like the Apollo program's mission control infrastructure — it was purpose-built to support a specific high-stakes mission at unprecedented scale, and its architectural patterns became the reference design that everyone in the field subsequently adopted.
words.techContext: When designing our internal ML platform, we used Uber's Michelangelo architecture as the reference: shared feature store, centralized model registry, and a unified training/evaluation pipeline that all ML teams are required to use.
words.exampleSentence: The Michelangelo paper's key lesson — that the highest-leverage investment in an ML platform is eliminating training/serving skew through a shared feature store — shaped our platform roadmap more than any other published design.
words.etymology: Named after the Italian Renaissance artist Michelangelo di Lodovico Buonarroti Simoni — the internal codename chosen by Uber's ML infrastructure team; described publicly in the blog post 'Meet Michelangelo: Uber's Machine Learning Platform' (September 2017).

words.shortDefinition: Airbnb's internal ML platform focused on reproducible experimentation and seamless research-to-production transition, introducing the ML project as a first-class artifact.
words.simpleDefinition: Bighead was Airbnb's internal ML platform, described in 2018. Its central innovation was treating the entire ML project — code, data pointers, feature definitions, model configuration, and evaluation results — as a single version-controlled artifact that could be reproducibly re-executed and safely promoted from a researcher's notebook to a production serving endpoint with minimal friction.
words.longDefinition: Airbnb's Bighead platform, described by Airbnb engineering in 2018, addressed a different pain point than Uber's Michelangelo. While Michelangelo focused on feature store parity and model serving at scale, Bighead focused on the research-to-production transition — the organizational process by which a model proven valuable in a researcher's notebook moves to a production serving system with all the correctness, reproducibility, and monitoring guarantees a production system requires. Bighead's central concept was the 'ML project' as a first-class artifact: a versioned bundle that captured all the inputs needed to reproduce a training run (data source pointers, feature definitions, model architecture code, hyperparameters) and all the outputs (trained model artifact, evaluation report, model card). This project artifact was the unit of deployment — moving a model to production meant promoting the project artifact through a lifecycle, not manually transferring files and configuration between systems. Key technical innovations: Bighead integrated directly with Airbnb's data infrastructure (Hive, Spark on Mesos) and feature store, supported both batch (offline) and real-time (online) inference, and provided an evaluation framework that compared candidate models against production baselines using standardized metrics. The platform's emphasis on researcher-facing tooling — making it easy for a data scientist with no platform engineering background to produce a production-ready model artifact — distinguished it from Michelangelo, which was more infrastructure-engineer-facing.
words.connector: Think of Bighead like a research-to-production conveyor belt — a researcher loads their model project at one end with all inputs and outputs fully documented, and the conveyor belt carries it safely to production through standardized quality gates, without the researcher having to understand the production infrastructure.
words.techContext: Our internal platform was influenced by Bighead's ML project concept: every training run produces a project artifact that bundles data version, feature config, model weights, and evaluation report into a single promotable unit.
words.exampleSentence: Bighead's insight that the ML project should be a first-class artifact with explicit data version pointers — not just a model file dropped in an S3 bucket — eliminated the 'works on my machine' problem for our research-to-production handoffs.
words.etymology: An internal codename — the name 'Bighead' was chosen by the Airbnb ML platform team as an irreverent reference to the scale of the problem it was solving; described publicly in the post 'Scaling Airbnb's Experimentation Platform' and subsequent MLOps conference presentations (2018–2019).
